djr-f1.accuracy_reason: The 'Ludus de morte Claudii' is the Apocolocyntosis. The quotation 'quis coacturus est?' comes from its first chapter.

djr-f101.accuracy_reason: Terence, Eunuchus prologue, line 41: 'nullumst iam dictum quod non dictum sit prius'.

djr-f1016.accuracy_reason: Horace, Ars Poetica 11: 'scimus, et hanc veniam petimusque damusque vicissim'.

djr-f1030.accuracy_reason: The ancient Vita Persi is attributed to Valerius Probus and contains 'editum librum continuo mirari homines et diripere coeperunt'. The note correctly describes the missing verb.

djr-f1076.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Ep. 88 does have 'monstras mihi qui sint modi flebiles; monstra potius quomodo inter adversa non emittam flebilem vocem', and Burton's English paraphrases it.

djr-f111.accuracy_reason: This is Virgil, Eclogue 3.8, the shepherds' exchange 'novimus et qui te transversa tuentibus hircis', which is an obscene taunt.

djr-f1129.accuracy_reason: Cyprian's Ad Donatum (ch. 6) attacks war; 'Madet orbis mutuo sanguine', quoted just after, comes from it.

djr-f1139.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.23–24 reads 'prima fere vota et cunctis notissima templis / divitiae'.

djr-f1140.accuracy_reason: Genius as a person's guardian spirit and appetite for enjoyment, and genium defraudare (Terence) meaning to stint oneself, are both correct.

djr-f116.accuracy_reason: In Martial 13.2 the sentence ends at 'ipse ego quam dixi.', and 'quid dentem dente iuvabit rodere?' begins a new one. So Burton breaks off mid-line, not 'in mid-sentence'. The omitted lines on Atlas and Latinus are correctly described.

djr-f1192.accuracy_reason: Intellectus agens is the scholastic-Aristotelian active intellect, and Burton uses it loosely as a gloss on 'soul'.

djr-f1208.accuracy_reason: In Lucian's Navigium (Ploion or Euchai), Timolaus wishes for magic rings, as Burton's text says.

djr-f1210.accuracy_reason: Morbus Neapolitanus was a standard early-modern name for syphilis.

djr-f1213.accuracy_reason: Mar del Sur is Spanish, Balboa's name for the Pacific, and Burton's spelling is a variant.

djr-f125.accuracy_reason: Proverbial (Gellius, praef.; Erasmus), and Lucretius 6 does say swine shun marjoram.

djr-f1296.accuracy_reason: Martial 12.61.10 has the singular 'scribit', of a drunken poet scrawling verses in charcoal and chalk on a dark archway that people use as a privy, so 'privy walls' is loosely right.

djr-f1300.accuracy_reason: The saying is proverbial (it is in Erasmus' Adagia). It goes back to Ennius' line 'qui ipse sibi sapiens prodesse non quit, nequiquam sapit', which Cicero quotes in Ad Familiares 7.6.

djr-f1304.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Epistles 1.18.29, a rich patron tells his poorer client 'meae stultitiam patiuntur opes': his wealth can afford his folly. Burton does twist this into 'wealth and folly go together'.

djr-f131.accuracy_reason: Plagiarius first meant a kidnapper, and Martial (1.52) uses it for a literary thief. Burton's 'a trifler, a trivant' does not translate the word.

djr-f1325.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Caligula 53, reports that Caligula called Seneca's writing 'harenam sine calce' (sand without lime).

djr-f1328.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Letters 115.1, reads 'quaere quid scribas, non quemadmodum'.

djr-f133.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Romans 14:5 reads 'unusquisque in suo sensu abundet'. Burton's version changes the mood and the word order.

djr-f1339.accuracy_reason: This is the closing sentence of the Phaedo, where Phaedo is speaking to Echecrates.

djr-f1341.accuracy_reason: In the Symposium (221c–d) Alcibiades says Socrates is like no one 'of the ancients or of those now living', and draws the comparisons with Achilles and Brasidas and with Nestor, Antenor and Pericles.

djr-f1359.accuracy_reason: Ammianus 23.6 says this of the Persians ('iudicatur is beatus... qui in proelio profuderit animam'). Burton's sidenote heads it 'de Parthis'.

djr-f1363.accuracy_reason: Georgics 4.441, on Proteus, reads 'omnia transformat sese in miracula rerum'.

djr-f1369.accuracy_reason: The translation of Adam of Bremen's Latin is accurate, and Burton's English is indeed loose.

djr-f1376.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Satires 2.3.300–302, Horace asks the Stoic Damasippus 'qua me stultitia, quoniam non est genus unum, insanire putas?'. Burton rearranges the lines.

djr-f1385.accuracy_reason: Suisset is Richard Swineshead, the fourteenth-century Oxford author of the Liber calculationum, known as 'the Calculator'. Pene is the late spelling of paene.

djr-f1387.accuracy_reason: In Timaeus 22b an Egyptian priest tells Solon that the Greeks are always children.

djr-f1388.accuracy_reason: Timaeus 22b has only 'you Greeks are always children'; the list of modern nations is Burton's own addition.

djr-f1397.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Germania 2 does read 'informem terris, asperam caelo, tristem cultu aspectuque', and Sabellicus clearly reverses it.

djr-f140.accuracy_reason: In Erasmus's colloquy Diversoria the German innkeeper tells a guest who complains to look for another inn. This matches the sidenote 'Erasm. dial.'

djr-f1420.accuracy_reason: In the Historia Augusta, Spartianus (Hadrian 18) says Hadrian had bankrupts flogged on the back in the amphitheatre ('catomidiari in amphitheatro').

djr-f1427.accuracy_reason: Claude de Seyssel wrote La Grand'Monarchie de France; Sleidan's Latin translation was published as De republica Galliae.

djr-f1430.accuracy_reason: Lucian (Against the Ignorant Book-Collector 13) does tell of Epictetus' lamp being sold for 3,000 drachmas. The word 'earthenware' is a detail I can't confirm: Lucian calls it only a clay or iron lamp in some versions, and the note states it as fact.

djr-f1432.accuracy_reason: The saying 'vox et praeterea nihil', said of a plucked nightingale, is well known (Plutarch's Spartan sayings), and Lipsius' phrase echoes it.

djr-f1437.accuracy_reason: This is Horace, Satires 2.3.78–80, and Horace does read 'tristive'. Calling the missing words the sentence's 'main verb' is loose, since 'calet' belongs to the relative clause, but nothing in the note is false.

djr-f1438.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Satires 2.3.165–166 the words 'ambitiosus et audax; / naviget Anticyram' do occur. Burton's line is close to a direct quotation, so 'echoes' undersells it, but the note is not wrong.

djr-f1439.accuracy_reason: Martial 3.76 is addressed to Bassus, who lusts after old women and scorns girls. The standard text does read 'non haec est mentula demens'.

djr-f1467.accuracy_reason: Quintilian 10.1.128 does have 'multa rerum cognitio' in the nominative, but 'omnem fere studiorum materiam' is accusative there as well. The 'multa probanda, multa etiam admiranda' comes later, at 10.1.131, so this is not one original sentence.

djr-f1473.accuracy_reason: Juno Moneta's temple on the Capitol held the Roman mint. That is correct.

djr-f1482.accuracy_reason: Plica polonica, a matting of the hair thought endemic in Poland, is correctly described.

djr-f1484.accuracy_reason: The words come from Cyprian, Ad Donatum, which asks the reader to look down on the world from a lofty watchtower ('in illa sublimi specula constitutus').

djr-f1485.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Ep. 13.16–17, does contain both 'semper incipit vivere' and 'foeda hominum levitas cotidie nova vitae fundamenta ponentium, novas spes etiam in exitu inchoantium'.

djr-f151.accuracy_reason: Quintilian 10.1.129 reads 'in eloquendo corrupta pleraque, atque eo perniciosissima quod abundant dulcibus vitiis'. The note quotes it correctly.

djr-f16.accuracy_reason: Diogenes Laertius 9.36 reports the saying, and Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 5.104, quotes it as Democritus' own words.

djr-f161.accuracy_reason: Gellius 19.3 has 'turpius esse... exigue atque frigide laudari quam insectanter et graviter vituperari'. The note quotes it correctly.

djr-f170.accuracy_reason: Ex Ponto 1.5.15–16 reads 'me quoque, qui feci, iudice digna lini'. The note is right that Burton's sidenote gives the wrong elegy number.

djr-f172.accuracy_reason: The line is Horace, Epistles 1.1.4, from the passage where he gives up verse after the Odes. Reading it as giving up lyric poetry is the usual view.

djr-f175.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.4.9–10, says Lucilius dictated two hundred verses an hour 'stans pede in uno'. The note is right.

djr-f178.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.19.2–3 does say that poems written by water-drinkers cannot please or live long, and the note rightly hedges the allusion with 'probably'.

djr-f18.accuracy_reason: Catullus 9.2 reads 'antistans mihi milibus trecentis', said of Veranius, the friend he prefers above 300,000 others; the change from participle to verb is described correctly.

djr-f186.accuracy_reason: The plucked-nightingale saying is in Plutarch's Sayings of Spartans (Moralia 233A), and the Latin form is a version of the Greek.

djr-f190.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Epistles 108.29 has the ox, the dog and the stork in one meadow; it is not about Pontus and has no maiden. The note's judgement is suitably hedged.

djr-f195.accuracy_reason: 'Topiarius' means an ornamental gardener, and the dogs lapping the Nile on the run for fear of crocodiles is a well-known proverb (Pliny, Phaedrus, Macrobius).

djr-f2.accuracy_reason: The passage is from Apocolocyntosis 1, and Seneca's next words, 'ego scio me liberum factum', are echoed in Burton's 'I am a free man born'.

djr-f200.accuracy_reason: The lines are Virgil, Eclogues 7.4–5, said of Corydon and Thyrsis.

djr-f21.accuracy_reason: In Cicero, Brutus 187, Antigenidas tells his pupil 'mihi cane et Musis'.

djr-f211.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 2.1.115–16 has the indicative 'promittunt medici'.

djr-f222.accuracy_reason: It is the usual explanation of the proverb (Horace, Epistles 1.18.15), and Burton does gloss it as 'moonshine in the water'.

djr-f223.accuracy_reason: The proverb comes from the story of Apelles and the cobbler (Pliny, Natural History 35.85).

djr-f230.accuracy_reason: Horace, Ars Poetica 410–11 has this wording and says it of natural talent and training.

djr-f239.accuracy_reason: In the Tablet of Cebes, Deceit (Apatē) gives everyone entering life a drink of error and ignorance. The note's 'cup of Error and Ignorance' is a fair summary of that.

djr-f24.accuracy_reason: The sidenote 'Praefat. hist.' points to the preface of Giovio's Histories, where he speaks of his long years at the papal court. Burton's own text sets his 30 years at Christ Church against this.

djr-f240.accuracy_reason: The line is Horace, Ars Poetica 140, 'quanto rectius hic qui nil molitur inepte', and it is said of Homer. Burton does turn it into a question.

djr-f249.accuracy_reason: This is the standard account of the andabatae: gladiators who fought blind in closed helmets.

djr-f250.accuracy_reason: Proverbs 26:4 in the Vulgate reads 'Ne respondeas stulto iuxta stultitiam suam'. The note quotes it correctly.

djr-f251.accuracy_reason: Pliny, Letters 10.96, does read 'Fuerunt alii similis amentiae'. Older editions numbered this letter 97, which matches Burton's sidenote.

djr-f260.accuracy_reason: The lines are Lucretius 3.1043–44 on Epicurus, where 'omnis' is the object of 'restinxit'. The note's remark on Burton's punctuation is correct.

djr-f262.accuracy_reason: Diogenes Laertius and Plutarch both record that Anaxagoras was nicknamed Nous ('Mind') because of his doctrine.

djr-f266.accuracy_reason: Lowering the fasces (fasces submittere) was the Roman gesture of deference, as the note says.

djr-f270.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 1.34.2–3 reads 'insanientis dum sapientiae / consultus erro', and it refers to Epicurean philosophy. Burton's own sidenote agrees.

djr-f287.accuracy_reason: The allusion to Lucius, turned into an ass in Apuleius' Golden Ass, is right. The reading of 'inverted' is suitably hedged.

djr-f288.accuracy_reason: The Sileni of Alcibiades come from Plato's Symposium 215 and Erasmus' adage 'Sileni Alcibiadis'. That adage itself describes inverted Sileni.

djr-f302.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.3.50–51 reads 'ille sinistrorsum, hic dextrorsum abit, unus utrique / error, sed variis illudit partibus'. Burton does leave out 'abit' and add 'omnes'.

djr-f313.accuracy_reason: The story of Hippocrates' visit to Democritus does come from the pseudo-Hippocratic letter to Damagetus, and Democritus is the speaker ('inquit').

djr-f320.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 6.848 has 'de marmore' and comes in Anchises' speech about the arts of other nations. Burton applies it to lifelike statues.

djr-f323.accuracy_reason: Persius 5.117 has 'servas'. Erasmus' Adagia collects 'Cretizare cum Cretensi' (lie to a Cretan, since Cretans were proverbial liars). 'Vulpinarier' means to play the fox.

djr-f324.accuracy_reason: This is the opening of Horace, Satires 1.1, and the standard text reads 'seu fors obiecerit'. The line continues with 'laudet diversa sequentis', as the note says.

djr-f345.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Epistles 1.2.42–43, the rustic waits for the river to run dry while it glides on for ever.

djr-f346.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 1.6 mocks an interminable 'Orestes' that has filled the margins and the back of the roll and is still unfinished.

djr-f349.accuracy_reason: Lucan 1.6–7 ('infestisque obvia signis / signa') describes civil war.

djr-f351.accuracy_reason: Seneca's lost De superstitione survives in fragments quoted in Augustine, City of God 6.10, including this passage.

djr-f352.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 1.3.38 reads 'caelum ipsum petimus stultitia'. Burton makes the verb passive.

djr-f360.accuracy_reason: Cicero, In Catilinam 1.30 has 'haec tam adulta rei publicae pestis', and the note hedges the identification appropriately.

djr-f361.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 9.641 has 'sic itur ad astra'. Burton's 'hac' and the irony are correctly described.

djr-f362.accuracy_reason: Insulsus does literally mean 'unsalted', hence 'witless'. 'Vos estis sal terrae' is Matthew 5:13.

djr-f363.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.15 reads 'quo me cumque rapit tempestas, deferor hospes'. Burton does change me to se.

djr-f364.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.41 reads 'unius ob noxam et furias Aiacis Oilei'. Burton cuts the line off before the name.

djr-f374.accuracy_reason: 'Sic itur ad astra' is Aeneid 9.641. Burton writes hac, and he means it ironically of the conquerors' fame.

djr-f377.accuracy_reason: Pro Milone 4.11 reads 'silent enim leges inter arma'.

djr-f379.accuracy_reason: Lucan 10.407 reads 'nulla fides pietasque viris qui castra sequuntur'. Burton does change nulla to rara and pietas to probitas.

djr-f381.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 2.12 reads 'quamquam animus meminisse horret', where Aeneas begins his account of Troy's fall.

djr-f389.accuracy_reason: In De anima 30, Tertullian calls plague, famine and wars a 'tonsura insolescentis generis humani'. Burton does answer 'sed ruina'.

djr-f394.accuracy_reason: Lucan 1.8 reads 'quis furor, o cives, quae tanta licentia ferri?' This comes in the poem's opening lament over civil war.

djr-f395.accuracy_reason: The source and the 'quare' point are right: Aeneid 7.340, Juno to Allecto. The last clause is confused, though. Juventus is singular in Virgil too; what Burton changed is the verbs, which he made plural (volunt, poscunt, rapiunt).

djr-f404.accuracy_reason: Agricola 30 reads 'auferre trucidare rapere falsis nominibus imperium'. Burton puts 'virtutem vocant' where Tacitus has imperium.

djr-f41.accuracy_reason: Persius 1.12 reads 'sed sum petulanti splene cachinno'. It was a common ancient belief that the spleen was the seat of laughter.

djr-f42.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.9.66 reads 'meum iecur urere bilis', and the liver was the seat of anger. The comment on Burton's following clause is fair.

djr-f421.accuracy_reason: Nicolaus of Damascus, the 'Damascen' of Burton's text, does report that the Celts thought it shameful to flee a falling wall or house.

djr-f422.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 7.461 reads 'saevit amor ferri et scelerata insania belli', and Burton's genitive 'scelerati' does attach the curse to the war.

djr-f428.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 8.96 reads 'cum Pansa eripiat quidquid tibi Natta reliquit', in a passage on provincial governors, and the note rightly hedges that Burton gives it loosely.

djr-f429.accuracy_reason: The pirate's retort to Alexander appears in Augustine, City of God 4.4, and in Cicero, De re publica 3 (a fragment).

djr-f447.accuracy_reason: In Juvenal 4.13–14 the thought 'nam quod turpe bonis… decebat Crispinum' is complete at Crispinum, and 'quid agas…' begins a new clause, so saying the quotation breaks off mid-sentence is questionable. The rest of the note is correct.

djr-f453.accuracy_reason: It reads the cry correctly as egging on both quarrelling parties, and Xanthippe was proverbially a shrew.

djr-f457.accuracy_reason: Petronius, Satyricon 116, gives 'aut captantur aut captant' (legacy-hunting at Croton) and the 'cadavera… corvi' comparison as separate sentences.

djr-f46.accuracy_reason: A succenturiator was a soldier added to fill up a century, a reserve or substitute, so the gloss is correct.

djr-f463.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Annals 4.18, on Silius and Tiberius, has 'dum videntur exsolvi posse'.

djr-f471.accuracy_reason: Manius Curius Dentatus was the byword for old Roman frugality, and the Bacchanalia were riotous revels. (The line is Juvenal 2.3.)

djr-f479.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.73 has the 'turba Remi', which 'sequitur fortunam… et odit damnatos', in the passage on Sejanus.

djr-f483.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 1.56: the complaisant husband who stares at the ceiling while his wife's lover is with her. The note identifies him correctly.

djr-f489.accuracy_reason: Utopia book 1 has the sheep that 'homines devorent ipsos... oppida vastent'. Burton paraphrases it, as the note says.

djr-f493.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 2.65–66: Aeneas tells Dido about Sinon's treachery, 'crimine ab uno disce omnis'.

djr-f495.accuracy_reason: In Cat. 1.32 Cicero wishes that what each man thinks of the republic were written on his forehead. The locus is right.

djr-f499.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.188 is 'multos da, Iuppiter, annos', and Seneca Ep. 10.5 reads 'quod scire hominem nolunt'. Both claims are correct.

djr-f50.accuracy_reason: Ars Poetica 334 ('aut simul et iucunda et idonea dicere vitae') and 344 ('lectorem delectando pariterque monendo') are correctly identified, and the substitution is correctly reported.

djr-f500.accuracy_reason: Persius 3.118 reads 'non sani esse hominis non sanus iuret Orestes'. The note quotes it and glosses it correctly.

djr-f502.accuracy_reason: Harpaste in Seneca Ep. 50 is correctly identified, and the note hedges suitably on the phrase itself.

djr-f503.accuracy_reason: Horace Epist. 1.2.38–39 is a question beginning 'nam cur'. 'est' does come from edo.

djr-f509.accuracy_reason: Clodius was notorious for the Bona Dea sacrilege and for adultery. The tag is Juvenal 2.27.

djr-f518.accuracy_reason: I recall the saying from Pliny's Natural History (book 18, on Cato), where the point seems to be practical gain from another's extravagance, such as buying a farm someone else has built up. The gloss 'learning by their mistakes' does not obviously fit that context, and the note does not say which Pliny work it means.

djr-f523.accuracy_reason: Catullus 22.21 reads 'sed non videmus manticae quod in tergo est', and the fable of the two wallets is Aesop's (Phaedrus 4.10).

djr-f527.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 3: Agamemnon says teachers must 'cum insanientibus furere' or be left alone in their schools ('soli in scholis relinquentur').

djr-f531.accuracy_reason: 'amabilis insania' is Odes 3.4.5–6 and 'mentis gratissimus error' is Epistles 2.2.140; both loci are correct.

djr-f534.accuracy_reason: Epistles 2.2.128–140 tells of the man of Argos who sat in an empty theatre imagining he heard tragedies; once cured, he says 'pol me occidistis, amici'.

djr-f535.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 6.283–284 reads 'clames licet et mare caelo / confundas'; 'surdo narrare' is proverbial and appears in Terence (Heaut. 222).

djr-f539.accuracy_reason: De Senectute 85 reads 'libenter erro; nec mihi hunc errorem... extorqueri volo', said of belief in the soul's immortality.

djr-f541.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 2 says those reared in the rhetoric schools can no more 'sapere' than kitchen-dwellers can smell sweet; the double sense of sapere is real.

djr-f547.accuracy_reason: Amphitryo prologue, line 35, spoken by Mercury: 'nam iuste ab iniustis petere insipientia est'.

djr-f563.accuracy_reason: In Tusculans 3.59 Cicero gives his own Latin version of lines from Euripides (Hypsipyle).

djr-f572.accuracy_reason: Satires 2.7.83–88; the Stoic sage as a smooth sphere is the standard reading of 'teres atque rotundus'.

djr-f575.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 13.26–27 continues: 'numera, vix sunt totidem quot / Thebarum portae vel divitis ostia Nili'.

djr-f576.accuracy_reason: The meanings of the names (forethought and afterthought) are correct, and the phrase reads as proverbial.

djr-f578.accuracy_reason: Asclepius 6 has 'magnum miraculum est homo'; Burton's 'homo sapiens' version is an elaboration of it.

djr-f579.accuracy_reason: It is a Greek proverb, quoted by Plato in the Phaedo (69c): 'many are the thyrsus-bearers, but few the Bacchoi'. The note's explanation is right.

djr-f584.accuracy_reason: Suisset is Richard Swineshead, 'the Calculator'. Vives mocks his kind of logical subtlety in De causis corruptarum artium, the work in Burton's sidenote.

djr-f59.accuracy_reason: Theriac (Venice treacle) did contain viper's flesh.

djr-f590.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Eclogue 3.36, reads 'insanire libet quoniam tibi'. 'Lubet' is the older form of 'libet'.

djr-f6.accuracy_reason: Phaedrus, prologue to book 5, reads 'novo si marmori adscripserunt Praxitelen suo'. The note's account of the change and of the forgery is right.

djr-f603.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.374: Aeneas speaks to his mother Venus, disguised as a huntress, about his troubles.

djr-f607.accuracy_reason: 'Salus populi suprema lex esto' is from Cicero, De legibus 3.8. Plato's Republic 4 (420b) holds that the aim is the happiness of the whole city, not of one class.

djr-f610.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Eclogue 9.28, reads 'miserae'. Mantua's lands were taken because they bordered Cremona's, which had been confiscated.

djr-f62.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.630 reads 'Non ignara mali', spoken by Dido to Aeneas.

djr-f643.accuracy_reason: De oratore 1.200 reads 'est enim sine dubio domus iuris consulti totius oraculum civitatis'. The quotation and locus are correct.

djr-f65.accuracy_reason: It is proverbial, and Juvenal 7.154 has 'crambe repetita'.

djr-f653.accuracy_reason: Plutarch, Cato Major 23: Cato mocked Isocrates' pupils as growing old in his school, as if to plead their cases before Minos in Hades.

djr-f66.accuracy_reason: Martial 1.53.12 reads 'stat contra dicitque tibi tua pagina "fur es"', addressed to the plagiarist Fidentinus. Burton does change the pronouns to 'mihi mea'.

djr-f664.accuracy_reason: In Livy 36.32 Quinctius compares the Achaeans in the Peloponnese to a tortoise drawn into its shell. Burton condenses this into a Latin tag.

djr-f672.accuracy_reason: The Virgil reference (Aen. 2.6–8) and the omitted middle line are right. But calling the second question 'unfinished in Burton's text' is misleading: Burton finishes it in English ('who is he that can sufficiently condole...'). The claim that it is Gerbelius's own wording also rests only on Burton's 'so he prosecutes it'.

djr-f678.accuracy_reason: Grotius's Mare Liberum (1609) argued for the freedom of the seas in the Dutch interest. The phrase was central to the Anglo-Dutch fishing disputes, so calling it a catchword is fair.

djr-f692.accuracy_reason: Herodotus 2.177 records Amasis's law that every Egyptian must declare his means of living each year. The Latin here is not Herodotus's wording.

djr-f698.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Annals 13.53 has these words and credits the Arar–Moselle canal plan to L. Antistius Vetus under Nero. Burton's 'Domitian' is therefore an error.

djr-f706.accuracy_reason: 'Sus Minervam (docet)' is in Erasmus's Adagia (1.1.40). The note's account of its sense and of how Burton applies it is correct.

djr-f707.accuracy_reason: The line is Terence, Andria 68: 'obsequium amicos, veritas odium parit'. The verjuice saying is a separate English proverb.

djr-f708.accuracy_reason: 'Augeae' is the correct genitive, and cleansing the Augean stables was proverbial for reforming deep-rooted abuses (it is in Erasmus).

djr-f71.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 2.1.117 reads 'scribimus indocti doctique poemata passim'.

djr-f713.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.1.63 reads 'iubeas miserum esse libenter', so Burton's 'stultos' does replace 'miserum'. The note is suitably hedged.

djr-f714.accuracy_reason: Ars Poetica 9–10 reads 'pictoribus atque poetis / quidlibet audendi semper fuit aequa potestas'. The note quotes it correctly, though it does not name the work.

djr-f716.accuracy_reason: In More's prefatory letter to Peter Giles, a theologian wants to be made bishop of Utopia and counts it 'sanctum ambitum'. The sense 'canvassing for office' is correct.

djr-f721.accuracy_reason: Cicero, De Officiis 1.22, gives the maxim as Plato's (Letter 9) and goes on to say that country and friends each claim a share in us.

djr-f742.accuracy_reason: The line comes from Cicero's De consulatu suo, and Cicero quotes it himself in De Officiis 1.77 and In Pisonem.

djr-f750.accuracy_reason: The passage matches Plutarch, Lycurgus 26, on elections to the gerousia ('not the swiftest among the swift…'). The note rightly hedges the identification.

djr-f758.accuracy_reason: 'Indulge genio' is in Persius 5.151, and the note explains genius correctly.

djr-f759.accuracy_reason: Athenaeus 14 (639c, citing Berosus) describes the Sacaea as a Babylonian feast in which servants rule their masters. The note's description is accurate.

djr-f761.accuracy_reason: In Historia Augusta, Hadrian 18.9, Hadrian orders that spendthrift bankrupts be 'catomidiari in amphitheatro'. The etymology and the explanation of the punishment are standard.

djr-f763.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 2.31 to 2.33 speaks of laws 'ipsis Veneri Martique timendas', in the passage on Domitian reviving the adultery law. The note is correct.

djr-f768.accuracy_reason: Politics 7.16 (1335a) recommends marriage at about 37 for men and 18 for women, so Burton's figures misreport Aristotle.

djr-f774.accuracy_reason: Boece's Scotorum Historia, book 1, describes the customs of the ancient Scots. Burton's main text does soften the rule to a ban on marriage.

djr-f781.accuracy_reason: The monte di pietà was a charitable pawn-lending institution that charged low interest.

djr-f785.accuracy_reason: The primum mobile was the outermost sphere in the Ptolemaic system, and its daily turning carried all the heavens. That fits Burton's use of it as a standard of measure.

djr-f795.accuracy_reason: Cicero, Philippics 5.5, has 'nervos belli, pecuniam infinitam'; the phrase is a common proverb for money.

djr-f8.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 1.85–86 ends with 'farrago libelli est'; Burton leaves out 'est', and the gloss on farrago is right.

djr-f80.accuracy_reason: Plautus, Aulularia 325, has 'homo trium litterarum' for 'fur' (thief).

djr-f800.accuracy_reason: Cicero (Ad Fam. 7.25) has 'manum de tabula'. In Pliny (NH 35.80), Apelles says he knew when to take his hand from a picture and Protogenes did not, so the note's short version is acceptable.

djr-f811.accuracy_reason: Ennius's line as Cicero quotes it (Pro Murena 30) reads 'pellitur e medio sapientia'. The proverb appears in Apocolocyntosis 1, a work traditionally attributed to Seneca.

djr-f813.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.8, describes the Iliad; the gloss on aestus is right.

djr-f814.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.14, reads 'quidquid delirant reges plectuntur Achivi'.

djr-f82.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 2.1.270, reads 'et piper et quidquid chartis amicitur ineptis'.

djr-f826.accuracy_reason: Seneca, De tranquillitate animi 17.10, attributes the saying to Aristotle.

djr-f829.accuracy_reason: 'Doctor Irrefragabilis' was Alexander of Hales's title. Occam was called 'Venerabilis Inceptor' and 'Doctor Invincibilis'. Scotus was the 'Subtle Doctor'.

djr-f833.accuracy_reason: The description of the tmesis is correct.

djr-f834.accuracy_reason: Anticyra was famous for hellebore, the classical remedy for madness.

djr-f840.accuracy_reason: The definition 'vir bonus dicendi peritus' (Cato, quoted by Quintilian) is the classical one, and the phrase does invert it.

djr-f842.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 10.640 describes the phantom of Aeneas that Juno makes. Burton's syntax allows the line to be read as said of the nightingale and then applied to the orator.

djr-f855.accuracy_reason: Epiphyllides are the small gleaning grapes. At Frogs 92 Aristophanes uses the word of feeble young poets, which matches Burton's sidenote.

djr-f872.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate wording of Job 28:13 is quoted correctly, and verse 12 asks 'Sapientia vero ubi invenitur?'.

djr-f881.accuracy_reason: Livy 21.4.9 reads 'has tantas viri virtutes ingentia vitia aequabant', said of Hannibal.

djr-f888.accuracy_reason: Persius 4.16 is correct, and Anticyra was famous for its hellebore.

djr-f899.accuracy_reason: In NH 36.75 Pliny calls the pyramids 'regum pecuniae otiosa ac stulta ostentatio'.

djr-f904.accuracy_reason: Metamorphoses 1.414 reads 'inde genus durum sumus'. The remark about the gloss is accurate.

djr-f911.accuracy_reason: Ulrich von Hutten's 'Nemo' does play on proverbs about 'no one' as praise of 'Nobody'.

djr-f915.accuracy_reason: Persius 1.110 reads 'per me equidem sint omnia protinus alba', and the sense given for 'white' is right.

djr-f917.accuracy_reason: The hellebore association and the reading of dolabra as boring the skull, matching Burton's gloss, are right.

djr-f918.accuracy_reason: At D.L. 7.127 Chrysippus says virtue can be lost through drunkenness and melancholy.

djr-f919.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.106–108 is quoted correctly. The changes Burton makes (ad summum, no est) are described accurately, and pituita does mean phlegm or catarrh.

djr-f920.accuracy_reason: Neuhaus's 1618 tract on the Rosicrucians has the subtitle 'An sint? Quales sint? Unde nomen illud sibi asciverint?'.

djr-f921.accuracy_reason: The Homer source is right: Odyssey 10.495, on Tiresias among the dead. But in Burton the line is the 'parasitical testimony of Dousa' about Lipsius, so it is Dousa who applies it; Burton quotes it ironically. The note credits the application to Burton.

djr-f93.accuracy_reason: Lucretius 3.11–12 does continue 'omnia nos itidem depascimur aurea dicta', addressed to Epicurus.

djr-f936.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Epistles 1.2.27, 'nos numerus sumus' means mere ciphers who make up the count, and Burton does turn it on himself.

djr-f943.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.4.103–105 is quoted correctly, and the omissions and change of word order are described accurately.

djr-f944.accuracy_reason: Martial 10.33.10 is 'parcere personis, dicere de vitiis'; 'licuit semperque licebit' is Ars Poetica 58.

djr-f948.accuracy_reason: Horace's line reads 'quamquam ridentem dicere verum / quid vetat?'. So 'quamvis' is Burton's substitute for 'quamquam', not something he added.

djr-f957.accuracy_reason: Eunuchus prologue 4–6 does continue 'responsum, non dictum esse, quia laesit prior', and the change of sense when Burton breaks off is correctly described.

djr-f962.accuracy_reason: Annals 15.68 has 'asperis facetiis… quae ubi multum ex vero traxere, acrem sui memoriam relinquunt'. The changes are described accurately, and so is Burton's English, which leaves out the clause about truth.

djr-f974.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Odes 4.1.15, 'centum puer artium' describes Paullus Fabius Maximus.

djr-f98.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Epistles 84.8 reads 'etiam si apparuerit unde sumptum sit, aliud tamen esse quam unde sumptum est appareat', in a passage on digesting what one reads.
